newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: SE Asian Cocoa - Prices withstand New York falls.
newsitem.headline: SE Asian Cocoa - Prices withstand New York falls.

text.p: Southeast Asian cocoa prices rallied on Wednesday as active trading was reported in Malaysia and Indonesia despite overnight falls in New York, dealers said.
A trader in Malaysia said the domestic market was not worried about the bearish tone of New York cocoa futures.
"It's just speculation-driven and not much of a fall," the dealer said.
Cocoa prices punched higher in Indonesia on shortcovering as buyers scrambled for beans to fill contracts, traders said.
"It's crazy," one trader in Indonesia said. "Some buyers are going up-country to buy the beans instead of waiting for them to come to town because they have outstanding contracts to fill."
"The easing of prices in New York had no real impact on the local market," he added. "At most, we will see growers and middlemen holding back, waiting for prices to pick up."
The May cocoa contract on the CSCE finished on Tuesday US$4 down on the day at $1,414 a tonne, near the floor of its $1,413-1,427 range. Most-active July eased $6 to $1,455 a tonne.
Malaysian traders said they had noted steady buying of small quantities of beans in the local market since last Wednesday by importers who had to honour contracts.
"Consumers in Malaysia appear reasonably stocked on imported beans in the near-term," said a trader in Kuala Lumpur. "The current buying appears to be mostly for spot delivery."
The Malaysian Cocoa Board quoted Standard Malaysian Cocoa (SMC) Grade 1 A out of Tawau, the country's main growing area, at an average of 3,420 ringgit a tonne, up 185 ringgit from last week.

The board quoted the SMC 1B grade out of Tawau at an average of 3,370 ringgit a tonne, up 185 ringgit from the previous week. Traders offered the SMC 1A at 3,370 ringgit a tonne and the SMC IB at 3,445-3,455 ringgit a tonne. In Indonesia, dealers said cocoa was quoted at 2,950-3,000 rupiah a kg in Ujung Pandang, capital of the key growing region of South Sulawesi, compared with 2,800-2,850 rupiah a week ago.
One trader said there had been an uneven flow of beans from some growing areas in South Sulawesi due to growers not carrying out proper crop maintenance and a lack of fertilisers.

"A tree which is well looked after will have beans in sizes that can be continually harvested over a few months. What I found in some places is that the tree has one large pod and several others which were very small," he said.
The trader said this resulted in long gaps between the time the pods can be harvested. But supplies seemed sufficient at the moment, with the main crop harvest proceeding without any problems.
